verses.zh: 祸哉，那些在床上图谋罪孽、造作奸恶的！天一发亮，因手有能力就行出来了。
verses.en: Beware wicked schemers,[NOTE:1] those who devise calamity as they lie in bed.[NOTE:2] As soon as morning dawns they carry out their plans,[NOTE:3] because they have the power to do so.
notes: Heb “those who think up evil.”
Heb “upon their beds.”
Heb “at the light of morning they do it.”

verses.zh: 他们贪图田地就占据，贪图房屋便夺取；他们欺压人，霸占房屋和产业。
verses.en: They confiscate the fields they desireand seize the houses they want.[NOTE:1] They defraud people of their homes[NOTE:2] and deprive people of the land they have inherited.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “they desire fields and rob [them], and houses and take [them] away.”
Heb “and they oppress a man and his home.”
Heb “and a man and his inheritance.” The verb עָשַׁק (ʿashaq, “to oppress”; “to wrong”) does double duty in the parallel structure and is understood by ellipsis in the second line.

verses.zh: 所以耶和华如此说：我筹划灾祸降与这族；这祸在你们的颈项上不能解脱；你们也不能昂首而行，因为这时势是恶的。
verses.en: Therefore the Lord says this: “Look, I am devising disaster for this nation![NOTE:1] It will be like a yoke from which you cannot free your neck.[NOTE:2] You will no longer[NOTE:3] walk proudly, for it will be a time of catastrophe.
notes: Heb “clan” or “extended family.”
Heb “from which you will not remove your neck.” The words “It will be like a yoke” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Or “you will not.”

verses.zh: 到那日，必有人向你们提起悲惨的哀歌，讥刺说：我们全然败落了！耶和华将我们的分转归别人，何竟使这分离开我们？他将我们的田地分给悖逆的人。
verses.en: In that day people will sing this taunt song to you—they will mock you with this lament:[NOTE:1] ‘We are completely destroyed;they sell off[NOTE:2] the property of my people.How they remove it from me![NOTE:3] They assign our fields to the conqueror.’”[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “one will lament [with] a lamentation [and] say.”tc The form נִהְיָה (nihyah) should be omitted as dittographic (note the preceding וְנָהָה נְהִי venahah nehi).
Or “exchange.” The LXX suggests a reading יִמַּד (yimmad) from מָדַד (madad, “to measure”). In this case one could translate, “the property of my people is measured out [i.e., for resale].”
Heb “how one removes for me.” Apparently the preposition has the nuance “from” here (cf. KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).

The Hebrew term שׁוֹבֵב (shovev, “the one turning back”) elsewhere has the nuance “apostate” (cf. NASB) or “traitor” (cf. NIV). The translation assumes an emendation to שָׁבָה (shavah, “captor”).tn Heb “to the one turning back he assigns our fields.”

verses.zh: 所以在耶和华的会中，你必没有人拈阄拉准绳。
verses.en: Therefore no one will assign you land in the Lord’s community.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “therefore you will not have one who strings out a measuring line by lot in the assembly of the Lord.”sn No one will assign you land in the Lord’s community. When judgment passes and the people are restored to the land, those greedy ones who disregarded the ancient land allotments will not be allowed to participate in the future redistribution of the land.

verses.zh: 他们（或译：假先知）说：你们不可说预言；不可向这些人说预言，不住地羞辱我们。
verses.en: “Don’t preach with such impassioned rhetoric,” they say excitedly.[NOTE:1] “These prophets should not preach of such things;we will not be overtaken by humiliation.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “‘Do not foam at the mouth,’ they foam at the mouth.” The verb נָטַף (nataf) means “to drip.” When used of speech it probably has the nuance “to drivel, to foam at the mouth” (HALOT 694 s.v. נטף). The sinful people tell the Lord’s prophets not to “foam at the mouth,” which probably refers in a derogatory way to their impassioned style of delivery. But the Lord (who is probably still speaking here, see v. 3) sarcastically refers to their impassioned exhortation as “foaming at the mouth.”

Heb “they should not foam at the mouth concerning these things, humiliation will not be removed.”tc If one follows the MT as it stands, it would appear that the Lord here condemns the people for their “foaming at the mouth” and then announces that judgment is inevitable. The present translation assumes that this is a continuation of the quotation of what the people say. In this case the subject of “foam at the mouth” is the Lord’s prophets. In the second line יִסַּג (yissag, a Niphal imperfect from סוּג, sug, “to remove”) is emended to יַסִּגֵנוּ (yassigenu; a Hiphil imperfect from נָסַג/נָשַׂג, nasag/nasag, “to reach; to overtake”).

verses.zh: 雅各家啊，岂可说耶和华的心不忍耐吗（或译：心肠狭窄吗）？这些事是他所行的吗？我―耶和华的言语岂不是与行动正直的人有益吗？
verses.en: Does the family[NOTE:1] of Jacob say,[NOTE:2] “The Lord’s patience[NOTE:3] can’t be exhausted—he would never do such things”?[NOTE:4] To be sure, my commands bring a rewardfor those who obey them,[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “house” (so many English versions); CEV “descendants.’
The MT has אָמוּר (ʾamur), an otherwise unattested passive participle, which is better emended to אָמוֹר (ʾamor), an infinitive absolute functioning as a finite verb (see BDB 55 s.v. אָמַר).
The Hebrew word רוּחַ (ruakh) often means “Spirit” when used of the Lord, but here it seems to have an abstract sense, “patience.” See BDB 925 s.v. 3.d.

Heb “Has the patience of the Lord run short? Or are these his deeds?” The rhetorical questions expect the answer, “No, of course not.” The people contest the prophet’s claims that the Lord’s judgment is falling on the nation.

Heb “Do not my words accomplish good for the one who walks uprightly?” The rhetorical question expects the answer, “Of course they do!” The Lord begins his response to the claim of the house of Jacob that they are immune to judgment (see v. 7a). He points out that the godly are indeed rewarded, but then he goes on to show that those in the house of Jacob are not godly and can expect divine judgment, not blessing (vv. 8-11). Some emend “my words” to “his words.” In this case, v. 7b is a continuation of the immediately preceding quotation. The people, thinking they are godly, confidently ask, “Do not his [God’s] words accomplish good for the one who walks uprightly?”

verses.zh: 然而，近来我的民兴起如仇敌，从那些安然经过不愿打仗之人身上剥去外衣。
verses.en: but you rise up as an enemy against my people.[NOTE:1] You steal a robe from a friend,[NOTE:2] from those who pass by peacefully as if returning from a war.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “Recently my people rise up as an enemy.” The MT is problematic in light of v. 9, where “my people” are the object of oppression, not the perpetrators of it. The form וְאֶתְמוּל (veʾetmul, “and recently”) is probably the product of fusion and subsequent suppression of an (ע) ʿayin. The translation assumes an emendation to וְאַתֶּם עַל (veʾattem ʿal, “and you against [my people]”). The second person plural pronoun fits well with the second plural verb forms of vv. 8b-10. If this emendation is accepted, then יְקוֹמֵם (yeqomem, the Polel imperfect of קוּם [qum]) should be emended to קָמִים (qamim; a Qal participle from the same root).

Heb “From the front of a garment glory [or perhaps, “a robe”] you strip off,” but this makes little if any sense. The term מִמּוּל (mimmul, “from the front of”) is probably the product of dittography (note the preceding word, which ends in [ם] mem) and subsequent suppression of ע (ʿayin). The translation assumes an emendation to מֵעַל (meʿal, “from upon”). The translation also assumes an emendation of שַׂלְמָה אֶדֶר (salmah ʾeder, “a garment, glory [or robe]”) to שֹׁלְמִים אֲדֶרֶת (sholemim ʾaderet, “[from] a friend the robe [you strip off]”). The MT’s אֶדֶר (ʾeder) is the result of improper division (the article has erroneously been attached to the preceding word) and haplography (of the final tav, which also begins the following word).

Heb “from those passing by peacefully, returnees from war.” Actual refugees, however, are probably not in view. The second line compares those who pass by peacefully with individuals returning from war. The battle is over and they do not expect their own countrymen to attack them.tc The passive participle שׁוּבֵי (shuve) is unattested elsewhere and should be emended to a participle שָׁבִים (shavim).

verses.zh: 你们将我民中的妇人从安乐家中赶出，又将我的荣耀从她们的小孩子尽行夺去。
verses.en: You wrongly evict widows[NOTE:1] among my people from their cherished homes.You defraud their children[NOTE:2] of their prized inheritance.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “women.” This may be a synecdoche of the whole (women) for the part (widows).
Heb “her little children” or “her infants”; ASV, NRSV “young children.”

Heb “from their children you take my glory forever.” The yod (י) ending on הֲדָרִי (hadari) is usually taken as a first person common singular suffix (“my glory”). But it may be the archaic genitive ending (“glory of”) in the construct expression “glory of perpetuity,” that is, “perpetual glory.” In either case, this probably refers to the dignity or honor the Lord bestowed on each Israelite family by giving them a share of his land to be inherited perpetually from one generation to another within each family. The term הָדָר (hadar) may refer to possessions that a person prizes (Lam 1:6).

verses.zh: 你们起来去吧！这不是你们安息之所；因为污秽使人（或译：地）毁灭，而且大大毁灭。
verses.en: But you are the ones who will be forced to leave![NOTE:1] For this land is not secure;[NOTE:2] sin will thoroughly destroy it![NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “Arise and go!” These imperatives are rhetorical. Those who wrongly drove widows and orphans from their homes and land inheritances will themselves be driven out of the land (cf. Isa 5:8-17). This is an example of poetic justice.
Heb “for this is no resting place.” The Lord speaks to the oppressors.
Heb “uncleanness will destroy, and destruction will be severe.”

verses.zh: 若有人心存虚假，用谎言说：我要向你们预言得清酒和浓酒。那人就必作这民的先知。
verses.en: If a lying windbag should come and say,[NOTE:1] ‘I’ll promise you blessings of wine and beer,’[NOTE:2] he would be just the right preacher for these people![NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “if a man, coming [as] wind and falsehood, should lie”; NASB “walking after wind and falsehood”; NIV “a liar and a deceiver.”
Heb “I will foam at the mouth concerning wine and beer.”
Heb “he would be the foamer at the mouth for this people.”

verses.zh: 雅各家啊，我必要聚集你们，必要招聚以色列剩下的人，安置在一处，如波斯拉的羊，又如草场上的羊群；因为人数众多就必大大喧哗。
verses.en: “I will certainly gather all of you, O Jacob,I will certainly assemble those Israelites who remain.[NOTE:1] I will bring them together like sheep in a fold,[NOTE:2] like a flock in the middle of a pasture;[NOTE:3] they will be so numerous that they will make a lot of noise.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “the remnant of Israel.”
The MT reads בָּצְרָה (batsrah, “Bozrah”) but the form should be emended to בַּצִּרָה (batsirah, “into the fold”). See D. R. Hillers, Micah (Hermeneia), 38.
The MT reads “its pasture,” but the final vav (ו) belongs with the following verb. See GKC 413 §127.i.

Heb “and they will be noisy [or perhaps, “excited”] from men.” The subject of the third feminine plural verb תְּהִימֶנָה (tehimenah, “they will be noisy”) is probably the feminine singular צֹאן (tsoʾn, “flock”). (For another example of this collective singular noun with a feminine plural verb, see Gen 30:38.) In the construction מֵאָדָם (meʾadam, “from men”) the preposition is probably causal. L. C. Allen translates “bleating in fear of men” (Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, and Micah [NICOT], 300), but it is possible to take the causal sense as “because of the large quantity of men.” In this case the sheep metaphor and the underlying reality are mixed.

verses.zh: 开路的（或译：破城的）在他们前面上去；他们直闯过城门，从城门出去。他们的王在前面行；耶和华引导他们。
verses.en: The one who can break through barriers will lead them out;[NOTE:1] they will break out, pass through the gate, and leave.[NOTE:2] Their king will advance[NOTE:3] before them;the Lord himself will lead them.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “the one who breaks through goes up before them.” The verb form is understood as a perfect of certitude, emphasizing the certainty of this coming event.
The “fold” from which the sheep/people break out is probably a reference to their place of exile.tn The three verb forms (a perfect and two preterites with vav [ו] consecutive) indicate certitude.
The verb form (a preterite with vav [ו] consecutive) indicates certitude.
Heb “the Lord [will be] at their head.”

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above.
Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

- First paragraph

- Second paragraph

- Third paragraph, etc.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- Micah 1-2 forms a literary unit. God's judgment on Samaria (the capital of Israel) should
have been a warning to Judah (cf. Ezek. 23)! See Introduction VII, B. #1-3

- As Micah 1 is in the literary form of a court scene, Micah 2 is in the literary form of a funeral dirge (i.e. "woe").

Special Topic: Prophecy (OT)

- This chapter has many similarities to the book of Amos, Micah's eighth century
contemporary to the Northern Ten Tribes.

OLD TESTAMENT TIMELINE

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: MICAH 2:1-5

1Woe to those who scheme iniquity,

Who work out evil on their beds!

When morning comes, they do it,

For it is in the power of their hands.

2They covet fields and then seize them,

And houses, and take them away.

They rob a man and his house,

A man and his inheritance.

3Therefore, thus says the Lord,

"Behold, I am planning against this family a calamity

From which you cannot remove your necks;

And you will not walk haughtily,

For it will be an evil time.

4On that day they will take up against you a taunt

And utter a bitter lamentation and say,

'We are completely destroyed!

He exchanges the portion of my people;

How He removes it from me!

To the apostate He apportions our fields.'

5Therefore, you will have no one stretching a measuring line

For you by lot in the assembly of the Lord."

2:1 "Woe" This INTERJECTIONS, "ah," "ha," mean "alas" (BDB 222, e.g. Isa. 1:4,24;
10:5; 17:12; 28:1; 55:1; Jer. 22:18; 34:5; Amos 5:16; 6:1). This is the characteristic literary
marker of a funeral dirge (i.e. a 3-2 beat in Hebrew poetry). As chapter 1 was replete with words of
lamentation and mourning (cf. Micah2:8,10,11,16), so chapter 2 continues this theme (cf. Micah2:4).

▣ "to those who scheme iniquity

Who work out evil on their beds" These are parallel lines of poetry. The first VERB
"scheme" (BDB 362, KB 359) and the second, "work out" (BDB 821, KB 950) are both Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLES.
This reflects the premeditated plans of evil Israelites (cf. Ps. 36:1-4; Prov. 23:7; Isa. 32:7). In this context it is referring to ways to
get more land from the poor rural farmers.

▣ "When morning comes, they do it" The VERB (BDB 793 I, KB 889, Qal IMPERFECT)
denotes continuing action. Sin starts in the thought life (cf. Hosea 7:6). The rabbis said our mind is like a plowed field ready for seed. What
our eyes see, our ears hear, and what our thoughts dwell, on becomes our actions!

▣ "For it is in the power of their hands" This is the OT equivalent of "might makes right." Just because we can does
not mean we should. There is an ethical God. He has made an ethical world. All humans will give an account to Him of their stewardship of
the gift of life (i.e. Matt. 25:31-46; Rev. 20:11-15)!

2:2 "They covet fields, and then seize them

They rob a man and his house,

A man and his inheritance" These are four parallel lines with strong VERBS.

- "covet" ‒ BDB 326, KB 325, Qal PERFECT with waw

- "seize" ‒ BDB 159, KB 186, Qal PERFECT with waw

- "take away" ‒ BDB 669, KB 724, Qal PERFECT with waw

- "oppress" ‒ BDB 798, KB 897, Qal PERFECT with waw

Remember, the extreme importance that the Jewish people placed on land inheritance within the Promised
Land (cf. Lev. 25:23; Num. 33:54; 36:1-12; Josh. 12-21). The land was meant to return to the original owners every fifty years
(i.e. Year of Jubilee; see Special Topic: Feasts of Israel, II. C.). YHWH's
gift to all the descendants of Abraham was now in the hands of greedy, wealthy exploiters. Micah, growing up and living in a small
rural community, had seen it again and again.

The term "house" can refer to a place of dwelling or to one's family (as could the term "inheritance"). These
exploiters wanted everything-land, children, adults, and all their property!

Special Topic: Hebrew Poetry, III. A. #4

2:3 "Therefore, says the Lord,

Behold, I am planning" The INTERJECTION "behold" (הב, BDB 243 II)
denotes a surprising statement of outcome. The UBS Helps For Translators series on Micah, says, "This is a way of showing that
something new and unexpected is about to happen" (p. 82).

This is irony. As evil humans plan (same VERB as was used in Micah 2:1, "scheme"), so too, God plans
(i.e. "we reap what we sow, e.g. see full list of Scripture texts at Gal. 6:7-10).

▣ "against this family" The term "family" means "clan" (BDB 1046). Notice the aggressive sin of some affects the complacent,
silent majority and the whole nation (cf. Amos 3:2) is judged!

▣

NASB
"calamity"

NKJV, TEV, NJB, REB, Peshitta
"disaster"

NRSV, LXX
"evil"

JPSOA
"misfortune"

This Hebrew term (BDB 949) means "evil," "distress," or "wickedness." In Exod. 32:12,14 it refers, as here, to the
judgment of God (cf. Deut. 29:112; Amos 9:4). It is used twice in Micah 2:3 and also in Micah 3:2,11.

▣ "you cannot remove your necks" The VERB (BDB 559, KB 561) is a Hiphil IMPERFECT.
This idiom of conquest is also used in Lam. 1:14; 5:5. It refers to a yoke on the neck of an ox which directs its activity.

▣ "walk haughtily" This is another IMPERFECT VERB (BDB 229, KB 246). Israel had become proud
and arrogant (i.e. see eighth century historical setting in Introduction). God will change their walk and mind about this (cf. Isa. 2:11,12).
Here (if literal), it refers to the shameful methods of the Assyrian exile.

Special Topic: The Path, The Way

2:4 "On that day" This refers to the time of God's visitation, here of judicial activity, sometimes, as here, it is temporal, other times
it is eschatological (i.e. the Day of YHWH.

Special Topic: That Day

▣ "taunt" This refers to a song or proverb (i.e. mashal, BDB 605 II, cf. Heb. 2:6, Peshitta), which others speak to
denote the current condition/situation of a person or group. It becomes a training tool for warning others not to do the same.

▣ "lamentation" This refers to a funeral dirge (BDB 624, KB 675, Qal PERFECT). The taunt
is Micah 2:4c-f (four lines of poetry).

This term (BDB 624, KB 675) is repeated three times in the Masoretic Hebrew Text:

- the VERB (Qal PERFECT with waw)

- the NOUN (MASCULINE SINGULAR)

- the NOUN (FEMININE SINGULAR)

This repetition denotes a grievous lamentation (wailing).

▣ "We are completely destroyed" This is a COGNATE
construction used for emphasis:

- BDB 994, KB 1418, a Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE

- BDB 994, KB 1418, a Niphal PERFECT

2:4 "He exchanges the portion of my people" The term "exchanges" (BDB 558, KB 560, Hiphil IMPERFECT)
is a legal term for the transfer of a land title. Thie VERB sounds similar to the VERB in the next line, "removes"
(BDB 559, KB 561, Hiphil IMPERFECT).

Verses 4 and 5 are the wail of the powerful, wealthy, influential Israelites (who stole from the poor) over the coming Assyrian
exile. But notice, it is not sorrow for their actions, but sorrow over the consequences of their actions. They are reaping what they sowed (in kind)!

▣

NASB, NKJV, NRSV
"How He removes it from me!"

TEV
"The Lord has taken our land away"

NJB
"no one else can restore it to them"

REB
"it is taken from us"

JPSOA
"How it slips away from me!"

LXX
"and there was none to prevent him

from turning away"

Peshitta
"there is none to restore our fields"

The MT is uncertain. Obviously the OBJECT is "the land" (lit. "our fields"). The problem, is the SUBJECT

- YHWH

- the invader

▣

NASB, Peshitta
"to the apostate"

NKJV
"to a turncoat"

NRSV
"our captors"

TEV
"to those who took us captive"

NJB
"to our despoiler"

REB
"to renegades"

JPSOA
"rebel"

JPSOA (footnote)
"ravager"

NET
"to the conqueror"

The MT has the ADJECTIVE "to apostate" (לשׁובב, BDB 1000),
but BDB suggestss reading it as "our captors" (שׁובינו, NET Bible). There is much confusion in
how to translate the "proverb" of v. 4. Here is a suggested translation from the UBS Text Project, p. 212:

"He exchanges the inheritance of my people! How will he
move (again) towards me, in order to make restitution for the fields which
he is distributing?"

"To the apostate He appoints our fields" can refer either to

- an apostate (i.e. one who turns back, BDB 1000, NKJV)

- JPSOA has "rebel" from "ravager," which denotes the Assyrian invaders
(from similar Hebrew root, BDB 1000, NRSV, TEV, NJB, NET Bible).

The irony is that these rich and powerful Israelite land grabbers are
calling others (i.e. the invaders) land grabbers.

2:5 "you will have no one stretching a measuring line" The LXX changes
the VERB "exchange" in the previous verse to "measure" to match
this line of poetry.

The word "measuring line" (BDB 286) basically means "cord." In
context the term can designate

- a line/cord used to measure a field, cf. Ps. 78:55; Amos 7:17; or "temple,"
Zech. 2:2 (i.e. BDB 286, #2)

- ones inherited land, cf. Deut. 32:9; Josh. 17:14; 19:9; 1 Chr. 16:18; Ps. 105:11;
Ezek. 47:13 (i.e. BDB 286, #3)

- measure in preparation to sell

- it is used as an idiom of judgment in 2 Sam. 8:2

▣ "For you by lot in the assembly of the Lord"
This refers to the sacred division of the Promised Land (Josh. 12-21). This statement is
tantamount to the powerful, wealthy, influential being excommunicated from the Promised
Land, both temporally and eschatologically (cf. Micah2:10). This passage implies that YHWH's
judgment to these exploiters is even more severe than Exod. 20:5; Deut. 5:9 ("visiting the
iniquity of the fathers on the children"). This exclusion is permanent and transgenerational!

▣ "by lot" The term "lot" (BDB 174) originally referred to the Urim and Thummim carried by the High Priest
on his chest behind the twelve stones. It is not certain what form this mechanical means of knowing YHWH's will was:

- different colored stones

- stones with "yes" or "no" painted on them

- stones with letters on them

- other unknown means

The NT word for "clergy" comes from this Hebrew concept.

Special Topic: Urim and Thummim

▣ "the assembly of the Lord" This is a covenant phrase. The Septuagint translates
the Hebrew term qahal (BDB 874) by the Greek term ecclēsia (gathering or assembly, which was later used by the

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: MICAH 2:6-11

6"Do not speak out," so they speak out.

But if they do not speak out concerning these things,

Reproaches will not be turned back.

7Is it being said, O house of Jacob:

'Is the Spirit of the Lord impatient?

Are these His doings?'

Do not My words do good

To the one walking uprightly?

8Recently My people have arisen as an enemy-

You strip the robe off a fellow-Israelite,

From unsuspecting passers-by,

From those returned from war.

9The women of My people you evict,

Each one from her pleasant house.

From her children you take My splendor forever.

10Arise and go,

For this is no place of rest

Because of the uncleanness that brings on destruction,

A painful destruction.

11If a man walking after wind and falsehood

Had told lies and said,

'I will speak out to you concerning wine and liquor,'

He would be spokesman to this people."

2:6-7 Verses 6-7 are dialogue. Micah speaks. It is hard to be certain where Micah starts and stops and where the rich,
speaking as a group, start and stop.

Leslie Allen (New International Commentary on the Old Testament), p. 292, has a good translation
of Micah 2:6 and 7: ". . .stop your preaching, they preach. They should stop preaching in this vein: humiliation won't overtake us: the
community of Jacob is party to the covenant. Has Yahweh lost His temper? Is this the way He acts? Do not His promises spell good
fortune? Do not we keep company with the One who keeps His word?"

Verses 6 and 7, to some extent, seem to reflect the rich's traditional covenant theology (much like Job's three
friends), but it fails to adequately understand the covenant requirements (cf. Lev. 26; Deut. 27-28; 30:15,19; i.e. known as "the two ways," cf. Ps.1).

2:6 "Do not speak out, so they speak out" There is a play (the VERB is repeated three times) on the term "speak
out" or "prophesy" (BDB 642, KB 694, Hiphil IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense, i.e "to drop a
message on someone," cf. Micah 2:6 [3 times, all Hiphil IMPERFECTS]; Micah2:11 [twice, also Amos 7:16]).

The term "speak out" is literally "to drip" (cf. Deut. 32:2; Ezek. 20:46; 21:2). It possibbly denotes an excited speaking with
spittle from the mouth (NET Bible). See Leslis Allen's translation above.

2:7 This verse has three (NASB, NKJV, JPSOA) or four (NRSV, TEV, NJB) questions. Who is speaking is uncertain. Some translations say

- the condemned rich of Judah (NET Bible)

- a false prophet (NKJV)

- YHWH Himself (Jewish Study Bible, p. 1208)

The JPSOA translates the first three poetic lines of v. 7 as follows:

"Is the House of Jacob condemned?"

Is the Lord's patience short?

Is such His practice?"

Qal PERFECT) it refers to the Lord's patience (cf. NRSV, TEV, NJB, NET Bible) or lack of anger (cf. Ps. 103:8-14).

2:8 "Recently My people have arisen as the enemy" The VERB (BDB 877, KB 1086) is a Polel IMPERFECT.
The covenant people have repeatedly broken their obligations to the Mosaic Covenant. This is what the exploiters refused to acknowledge! God's people
were acting like an invading enemy against their own covenant brothers and sisters (i.e. JPSOA footnote "e").

The problem in translating this phrase is that the MT is using "my people" as the attackers and exploiters, when in the following
lines they are the exploited.

Several translations emend the MT to "but you rise up against my people as an enemy" (cf. NRSV, TEV, NJB, NET Bible). See the
extended textual note in the UBS Text Project, vol. 5, p. 314.

Special Topic: Covenant

▣ "You strip the robe off a fellow-Israelite" The VERB (BDB 832, KB 980) is a Hiphil IMPERFECT.
This reflects the continuing action of the rich in exploiting the poor. This passage reflects the greed and heartlessness of the wealthy, influential,
Israelite land grabbers in evicting poor people from their houses and taking their clothes (even their children) as a guarantee for money borrowed (cf. Exod. 22:26,27).

Notice the groups impacted by this exploitation:

- covenant brothers, Micah 2:8b-c

- military veterans, Micah 2:8d

- covenant women, Micah 2:9a-b

- covenant children, Micah 2:9c

Two possible interpretations of this ambiguous phrase:

- that when Jewish soldiers (JPSOA) returned home from fighting foreign enemies (potential invaders and land grabbers) they thought

2:9 "The women of My people you evict" The VERB (BDB 176, KB 204, Piel IMPERFECT)
means "to drive out" (cf. Hosea 9:15). This implies that the husbands have already been sold into indentured servitude, now the wife.

▣ "From her children you take My splendor forever" These children become slaves and worse (as did their parents). Their
rightful land inheritance (here called "My splendor") as YHWH's covenant people in the Promised Land (i.e. Year of Jubilee, when land was to
be returned to its original tribal owners; see Special Topic: Feasts of Israel, II. C.) was lost to
greed and exploitation. They will also be corporately affected by the judgment of God (i.e. exile) that will come to national Judah, as it did to Israel.
But in the future, they will receive their inheritance again (cf. Micah2:5). So "forever" is a way of showing intensity, not time here.

This may simply be imagery of the policies of the Assyrian army of killing the very young (and the very old) before exiling the parents.

IMPERATIVES. This reflects either

- a warning to the faithful few (i.e. the remnant; see Special Topic: Remnant [three senses])

- more probably, YHWH's judgment of the nation (i.e. exile)

- YHWH speaks to the invaders (NET Bible)

▣ "this is no place of rest" This term is used of the Promised Land in Deut. 12:9; Ps. 95:11. Here, it is an idiom for invasion and exile.

▣ "Because of the uncleanness that brings on destruction" This term "uncleanness" (BDB 380) is used in the OT to
describe the abominations of the Canaanites. There is some question whether the MT has a VERB (BDB 379 I) or the
NOUN (BDB 380). The UBS Text Project gives the VERB an "A" rating. Micah uses this same term to
accuse the people of God of similar acts (cf. Lev. 18:24ff) that caused God to remove the Canaanites (cf. Gen. 15:12-21). He now removes the Israelites.

This verse has another COGNATE construction:

- VERB, BDB 287 II, KB 285, Piel IMPERFECT ("bring a destruction")

- NOUN, BDB 287, KB 285 ("a painful destruction")

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: MICAH 2:12-13

12"I will surely assemble all of you, Jacob,

I will surely gather the remnant of Israel.

I will put them together like sheep in the fold;

Like a flock in the midst of its pasture

They will be noisy with men.

13The breaker goes up before them;

They break out, pass through the gate, and go out by it.

So their king goes on before them,

And the Lord at their head."

2:12-13 These verses are a radical change from judgment to hope, which characterizes this book. There have been several theories
concerning this radical change:

- John Calvin and Kimchi see Micah 2:12 and 13 as referring to the deportation into exile

- it is possibly another quote from the false teachers (i.e. a response to Micah 2:10; Ibn Ezra)

- this is Micah's personal hope in YHWH's protection (Aramaic Targums)

- YHWH or Davidic Messiah as the good faithful Shepherd (i.e. Ps. 23; John 10)

- an insertion of the later redactor

- I prefer the sudden shifts to the poetic parallelism known as antithetical parallelism,
so common in Hebrew Wisdom Literature, and prophetic poetry.

Special Topic: Hebrew Poetry

2:12 "I will surely assemble all of you, Jacob" This is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and IMPERFECT
VERB from the same root (BDB 62, KB 74) for the "surety of YHWH's promise" of return and covenant blessing. This is a promise
of future restoration to the Promised Land through YHWH's power by YHWH Himself (cf. Deut. 30:4; Jer. 23:3; 31:8). Even though Israel
was judged because of the wicked, all of its people paid the price of invasion and exile. God will set it straight for those (and their descendants)
who truly trust and obey Him (i.e. the faithful remnant)!

Verse 12 is in the first person ("I"), but Micah 2:13 is in the third person. This is common in Hebrew, but here, possibly
Micah 2:12 is YHWH speaking and Micah 2:13 Micah's comment and development.

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

▣ "the remnant of Israel" This theological concept becomes a recurrent hope in the Prophets. It refers to a small group
of faithful, believing, obedient, covenant Israelites from which YHWH will build His kingdom (cf. Micah 4:6-7). The majority of the covenant
people (i.e. descendants of Abraham) are not believers, not obedient, and not right with God. They deserve temporal and eschatological judgment.

Special Topic: The Remnant (three senses)

▣ "like sheep in the fold,

Like a flock in the midst of its pasture" This may be a play on

- a place name, Bozrah (MT, JPSOA, BDB 131 II), which was known for its excellent sheep

- a parallel to a pasture and, therefore, a protected enclosure (BDB 131 I, found only here in the OT, i.e. sheepfold, which requires an emendation
to the MT using an Arabic root, "in a fold")

- other options, the LXX has "like sheep in affliction"; Peshitta, "like sheep when they are in danger." This option is also followed by the Latin Vulgate.

These allusions to sheep and shepherding are covenant imagery for YHWH's care and provision (cf. Psalm 23; also Messianic in John 10).
The sheep are guarded and cared for. The last line of Micah 2:12 seems to imply

- a joyful group

- as in NKJV and NIV, a large number of people

2:13 Micah seems to be speaking again (i.e. third person references to YHWH). This verse is Messianic text. The Davidic kingship will
be restored (cf. 2 Samuel 7; 1 Chronicles 17).

There is a word play between "breaker" (Micah 2:13a, BDB 829, KB 971, Qal PARTICIPLE) and "break out"
(Micah 2:13b, BDB 829, KB 971, Qal PERFECT). The king will lead his people out of the pen of the exile into a large pasture,
where they run and jump with joy!

Notice the concept of pen is used in two senses:

- in Micah 2:12 as a protective enclosure

- in Micah 2:13 as a restrictive enclosure

Notice how the Davidic King (cf. Micah 2:13c) is paralleled with YHWH (cf. Micah 2:13d). This implies a divine king (cf. Micah 5:2-4)!
However, this context could be seen as YHWH, the One who caused the exile is the very One who reverses it. The king may be a way of referring to YHWH (cf. Micah 4:7; 1 Sam. 8:7).

Special Topic: OT Titles of the Special Coming One

▣ "the gate" This was Old Testament imagery for the power of a city or city-state. This is a word play between the gate of the sheepfold and
the national power (i.e. Assyria), which exiled the Northern Ten Tribes (in 722 B.C.).
